new_statements.translation: The Bocotá of Chiriquí manifests itself as an accentual language. On this plane, the accent consists of the increase in intensity that a syllable acquires within a word or, as will be seen below, within a [phrase] ... Having thus established the Bocotá of Chiriquí as an accentual language of the ... is accented, that is, it represents a prominence of intensity in the ...

new_statements.locator: Google Books search-inside snippets of the 1996 ELC volume (id R8waAQAAIAAJ), page not shown; article runs pp. 7-26
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. The quoted passage is present in (Google Books id R8waAQAAIAAJ = Estudios de Lingüística Chibcha 1996, i.e. Margery Peña 1996) and feed2.xml, exactly as the reader gives it apart from cosmetic differences: Google's scanned puts spaces before punctuation ('acentual. En este plano, el acento') and the reader joined the feed1 and feed2 snippets with '[...]' where Google prints '... '. The Margery 1989 tonal note is also verified in the held PDF text (page image headed '72 REVISTA DE FILOLOGIA Y LINGUISTICA', note 7): 'el bocotá -hasta el estado actual de nuestras investigaciones en este campo- se nos ha revelado como una lengua tonal, de bajo rendimiento, con dos tonos fonemáticos…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Margery's mature (1992-1996) analysis: Buglere/Bocotá is a stress-accent language, not a tone language; each polysyllabic word heard in isolation has one syllable of intensity prominence (Narraciones bocotás 1992 / Mitología 1994 note, snippet). Where that syllable falls is NOT stated in anything I could open; the Margery 1996 forms reproduced by Chevrier 2017 (pp. 369-372) carry the acute on varying syllables (biúsi, ɡuáɡaba, dái, badá, ɡiɾɔ́ɡɾɔ, daɡɛ́, tãʤuɡádɛ), which is consistent with lexically determined placement but is my inference, not a source statement. The earlier Margery 1989 note (held PDF, p. 72) analysed the same variety as a low-yield two-tone language (high vs low), and Chevrier 2017 lists Buglere among the Chibchan languages where tone vs accent remains an open question.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened text.
new_statements.exceptions: Margery 1994 (snippet): at phrase level the prominence 'no se percibe en algunos términos bisilábicos'. Gunn & Gunn 1974 (snippet) describe a phrase accent (acento de frase, marked ') that is weaker than sentence accent, with final-syllable lengthening as the most consistent phrase cue and four phonological phrase types.
new_statements.domain_note: Margery: word-level prominence in citation forms, with phrase-level reduction; Gunn & Gunn 1974 work at the phonological-phrase and sentence level. Margery 1989 (full text on file, p. 72): 'el bocotá -hasta el estado actual de nuestras investigaciones en este campo- se nos ha revelado como una lengua tonal, de bajo rendimiento, con dos tonos fonemáticos, uno alto y otro bajo' — later abandoned by the author.
new_statements.identity_note: All of Margery Peña's work (1988-1999) describes the 'bocotá de Chiriquí' variety (Chiriquí province / Costa Rica border area, informants such as Francisco Rodríguez Atencio); Gunn & Gunn 1974 (SIL) describe Bocotá in central Panama (HLAS: 'some 1,500 speakers located in central Panama and divided...'), i.e. the Bocas del Toro/Veraguas side. Glottolog has no separate dialect codes; both fall under bugl1243. Ethnonym/glossonym variants: Buglere, Bocotá, Bokota, Bogota, Murire, Sabanero.
